dailyBrief.text: Solon woke up clear and cold at 39°, but it turns into a sunny, dry Saturday with a high near 65° and no rain — a perfect fall day. Overnight the Brewers edged the Rays 3-2 in World Series Game 1, with Game 2 tonight at 8 PM, while Friday's market drop is still the big money story: the Dow fell 653 points as oil spiked. Today is packed close to home: Barack Obama rallies in Cleveland for Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, the Solon library hosts a hands-on chemistry morning for kids at 10:30, the City of Solon Trick-or-Treat Trail runs 4–6 PM, and the Cavs play their home opener against Brooklyn at Rocket Arena at 7:30 PM.

weekBrief.text: It's a golden fall week ahead in Solon: mostly sunny and dry, highs in the mid-60s warming to the low 70s by Thursday, lows in the 40s, and no real rain in the forecast until late next weekend. The weekend is full — the Cavs' home opener tonight and the Browns at Tennessee on Sunday, the North Union Farmers Market season finale in Chagrin Falls on Sunday morning, and the Cavs back home against Minnesota on Monday — and Halloween lands next Saturday with Ohio State at USC that night. The standout deal is still Miles Farmers Market's jumbo eggs at $1.00 a dozen, good through Tuesday. And with the baby due in early November, this week is for finishing touches and enjoying the calm.

U.S. pulls diplomats back as intelligence warns Iranian plots against Americans have advanced
items.summary:
A senior U.S. intelligence official has warned that Iran has sharply stepped up efforts to target American personnel abroad, and that lethal plotting has reached an advanced stage in the Middle East and in some other countries as well. The warning, in an October 23 memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, was first reported by Axios and was seen by Reuters.

The alert follows a week of pullbacks at American missions in the region. The State Department ordered non-emergency staff and families out of diplomatic posts in Saudi Arabia after intensified attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi forces, planned to withdraw family members from several other missions, and on Saturday updated travel advisories for more than a dozen Gulf and Middle East countries, including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel. Officials said staffing choices are constantly reassessed as new security information arrives, and many diplomats who had only recently returned after earlier evacuations during the Iran war are now leaving again.

The memo did not name specific targets or the countries outside the Middle East where plotting was detected, so the immediacy of any single attack remains unclear. Even so, U.S. officials described the threat level for Americans in the region as the highest since the war began in February, coming alongside a rise in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

What to watch is whether the drawdown expands into full departures from more embassies, and whether Washington links the warning to any new military action. Iranian officials have previously been reported to be preparing a more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale strikes.

items.title: France floods streets with 70,000 police as cost-of-living protests return for a second weekend
items.summary:
France mounted a huge security operation on Saturday as students, workers and unions returned to the streets over living costs and strained public services. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez mobilized about 70,000 police nationwide, roughly 10,000 more than a week earlier, and told officers in Paris to be hyper-reactive to troublemakers and looters.

Soldiers from an anti-terrorism unit patrolled the Champs-Elysees while police vans circled the Arc de Triomphe to protect landmark sites. Luxury stores around Place Vendome boarded up and added private security, museums in Paris closed for the day, and authorities restricted the main march and banned non-union demonstrations in several city centers after the October 17 protests turned into vandalism, looting and clashes.

The government is trying to separate two things at once: a broad, largely peaceful movement angry about prices, schools and public services, and smaller groups officials say exploit the marches for chaos. Protest organizers make the opposite argument, saying bans and a heavy military presence are an attack on the right to protest while the underlying grievances go unanswered. Similar anti-war and cost-of-living protests also swept Italian cities on Saturday, and student protests in Albania turned violent in Tirana.

What to watch is whether Saturday stays mostly calm under the show of force, and what President Emmanuel Macron offers next. He met student representatives on Friday and promised more teachers and an overhaul of the university admissions system, but student groups said protests would continue until concrete proposals arrive.

items.title: Drone strikes have killed at least 306 people in Sudan in three weeks, U.N. says
items.summary:
Drone attacks killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more across Sudan in just the first three weeks of October, the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said on Friday. He condemned the escalation and said drones now account for the majority of civilian deaths in Sudan's civil war this year.

The U.N. human rights office said strikes attributed to both sides — the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces — have hit homes, markets, health centers, shelters for displaced people, power plants and other basic infrastructure. The attacks have spread across Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile and Khartoum, and include a repeated strike on a transport truck in West Kordofan that killed at least 139 people and a strike on a hospital in Blue Nile that forced the facility to close.

Sudan's war began in April 2023 and has forced about 13 million people from their homes, in what aid groups call the world's largest humanitarian crisis. Turk said the pattern of hitting civilian objects is driving new displacement and destroying the services people depend on, and he called on both parties to respect international humanitarian law and halt the arms transfers fueling the fighting.

What to watch is whether the U.N. Security Council can agree on any response. The United States on Friday urged the Council to push for a humanitarian truce and expand an arms embargo, but China and Russia opposed widening the embargo.

items.title: Ukraine and Russia agree to a local ceasefire at Oleshky, swap 270 prisoners each, and set new peace talks
items.summary:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to stop fighting in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky starting October 27, in a deal the White House said was brokered through First Lady Melania Trump. The pause is meant to let humanitarian aid in and let residents leave through designated corridors, after locals reported a deepening food crisis in a town occupied since February 2022.

The agreement is narrow, but it arrived with two other steps. The two sides also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the first such swap since August, which President Volodymyr Zelenskiy called a very important result. And Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to hold technical-level meetings in the first half of November, in Abu Dhabi or possibly Switzerland, with hopes that a leaders' meeting could eventually follow.

The diplomacy follows weeks of friction between Washington and Kyiv, including limits placed on the Starlink system Ukraine uses for frontline communications and protection against incoming attacks. President Donald Trump said Friday he would get any continuing Starlink problem straightened out, if necessary by speaking directly with Elon Musk, and Ukrainian officials have since reported that operating speeds were restored.

What to watch is whether the Oleshky pause actually takes hold on Monday and whether the November talks get anywhere on the core dispute. Previous U.S.-led rounds stalled in February, Moscow still demands that Ukraine surrender the entire Donbas, including land Russia has not captured, and Kyiv still rejects giving up territory it controls — even as fighting and strikes on energy and industrial targets continue elsewhere.

items.title: Eight foreign ministers meet in Istanbul and warn Washington and Israel against new strikes on Iran
items.summary:
Foreign ministers from eight countries — Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, joined by Britain, France, Germany and Italy — met in Istanbul on Friday in a brand-new diplomatic format and urged the United States and Israel not to resume attacks on Iran. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, who co-convened the summit, said a new attack would widen the war across the region and that military intervention is by no means a solution.

The ministers called for a diplomatic settlement, backed the June memorandum of understanding that was meant to pave the way to a final agreement, and demanded unrestricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz. They also condemned attacks on civilians and commercial vessels and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The diplomatic push comes as October has become the worst month on record for attacks on shipping in and around Hormuz, with 28 confirmed or reported incidents this month and more than 30 large crude tankers damaged since the war began in February.

The two groups did not speak with one voice on everything. Germany's foreign minister held Iran and the Houthis responsible for the instability, while the four regional countries issued a joint statement naming Israeli occupation as the main source of instability in the region. Neither the United States nor Iran took part in the meeting.

What to watch is whether this format becomes a real channel or just a statement. The ministers agreed to meet regularly, with the next session planned in Germany, but any reopening of Hormuz still depends on Washington and Tehran, whose own negotiations remain stalled over Iran's conditions and its nuclear program.

items.title: Israel votes Tuesday with final polls split — neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to a majority
items.summary:
Tens of thousands of Israelis living overseas are flying home to vote in Tuesday's parliamentary election, because Israel generally does not allow citizens abroad to cast absentee ballots. Organizers estimate more than 50,000 expatriates will return for the October 27 vote, some spending thousands of dollars on flights and hotels for a single ballot.

They are returning to an election with no clear winner. Final television polls published October 22 and 23 disagree sharply: three surveys put former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud as the largest party, with the anti-Netanyahu bloc at 52 to 56 seats and Netanyahu's bloc at 50, while a fourth survey put Likud well ahead and Netanyahu's bloc as high as 59 seats. A governing majority in the 120-seat Knesset requires 61 seats, and no survey gave either principal bloc that number on its own.

The campaign has turned on the Gaza war, national security, military conscription for the ultra-Orthodox, and accountability for the failures around the October 7, 2023 attacks. Eisenkot, who is positioning himself as a centrist alternative focused on unity and reform, has even discussed the possibility of a minority government if the numbers fall short, while small parties hovering near the 3.25 percent threshold could decide who gets to try to form a coalition at all.

What to watch after Tuesday is not just who finishes first, but the coalition math. With Arab parties holding a projected 14 to 16 seats counted separately from both blocs, government formation could take weeks of negotiation — and another election cannot be ruled out if no one assembles 61.

items.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska from certifying its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses
items.summary:
The Justice Department has sued in federal court in Anchorage to stop Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate result if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses narrowly, arguing that voters could be confused by another candidate on the ballot with a nearly identical name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. President Donald Trump took credit for the move on Friday, telling reporters he was the one who said to do it.

The department is asking a judge to halt certification long enough for an investigation into whether votes cast for the second Sullivan were actually meant for the senator, a question it says Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation could magnify. In the primary, Democrat Mary Peltola led with about 49.5 percent, Senator Sullivan had about 41.4 percent, and Daniel J. Sullivan took about 2.5 percent, roughly 4,107 votes — so the lawsuit only matters if the November margin is smaller than that third candidate's total.

Alaska officials and courts already rejected attempts to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot earlier this year, he denies being planted by Democrats and says he is running because he dislikes the incumbent's record, and multiple legal scholars have called the federal theory novel and doubtful. Peltola criticized the intervention, while the senator's campaign said Alaskans can tell the candidates apart and it would let the complaint proceed.

Why it matters is the precedent. This is a preemptive federal challenge filed before a single general-election vote has been counted, in a race that could decide Senate control, and critics — including some Republican election officials — see it alongside the administration's California ballot demands as a sign the government is preparing to contest close midterm results more broadly.

items.title: Trump's foreign policy is hitting voters in the wallet — and Republicans are starting to distance themselves
items.summary:
A Reuters analysis published Saturday argues that President Donald Trump's moves abroad have become a kitchen-table problem at home, imperiling Republicans in the midterms. Voters rank foreign policy low as a standalone issue, but polling shows most Americans connect the Iran war and tariffs directly to the higher prices they are paying.

The numbers behind that connection are stark. Gasoline averages $4.27 a gallon, nearly 40 percent higher than a year ago, consumer prices accelerated in September as fuel costs surged, and the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found most Americans believe the administration's foreign policy has hurt the country's global standing and their own household finances. Senior Iranian officials told Reuters Tehran is deliberately trying to keep oil prices high and prolong the diplomatic stalemate to hurt Trump in November, including with new tactics against ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Some Republican candidates have begun putting distance between themselves and the president on the Middle East conflict, the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine. The White House counters that Trump was always clear there would be temporary market disruption from the Iran conflict, and that his economic record still beats the Democratic alternative.

What to watch in the final ten days is whether that distancing spreads. Midterms are usually a referendum on the president in power, and if voters keep treating foreign policy as an economic issue, Republican candidates in close races have to decide whether standing with Trump costs more than breaking with him.

items.title: More than 21 million Americans have already voted, with early turnout running ahead of the last two midterms
items.summary:
Almost 21 million people had already cast midterm ballots by Friday morning, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, and the total was climbing by about 2 million votes a day. The count combines mail ballots returned and in-person early votes, and updated tracking through Saturday put the figure above 23 million.

University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald, who runs the Election Lab, said state-by-state turnout is running ahead of both the 2022 midterms and 2018 — and 2018 was the highest-turnout midterm since 1914. In states that report party data, Democrats are voting early at higher rates than Republicans, turnout is also up among unaffiliated voters, and in states such as North Carolina and Georgia, voters of color are showing up in large numbers. Ohio alone had passed 920,000 early ballots, up about 30 percent over 2022 in one analysis.

Both parties are reading the tea leaves carefully, because early voting is a notoriously poor predictor of final results — it mostly shows who is enthusiastic, not who will win. Democrats point to affordability anger energizing their base, while some Republican strategists privately worry about a soft undertow of GOP voters staying home over gas prices, foreign conflicts and tariffs.

What to watch is the final week. Texas, Florida, Georgia and North Carolina have each already banked more than a million early votes, Georgia's early total alone is over 40 percent of its entire 2022 turnout, and Election Day voting on November 3 will still decide whether the early Democratic edge holds or gets swamped.

items.title: The MAHA-MAGA alliance is fracturing, with $100 million promised and only about $4 million spent
items.summary:
Leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement promised to cement their alliance with President Donald Trump's movement by spending $100 million to help Republicans in the midterms. Instead, allied MAHA super PACs and nonprofits have spent only about $4 million supporting candidates since January 2025, according to federal election filings reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The donors who powered the movement last cycle are largely missing. Mark Gorton, who gave more than $1 million to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s 2024 presidential bid and is listed as a co-president of the MAHA PAC, told the Journal at a recent Washington event that this is not an important election and that he does not really like being involved in politics. Despite voting for Trump in 2024, Gorton is a registered Democrat, and this cycle he has donated to Democratic groups.

Former Kennedy aides say the disappointment is about policy, not just money. They point in particular to Trump's move to boost production of the herbicide glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, on national-security grounds, and argue that few of the movement's promises were kept — leaving Kennedy's political operation too frail to deliver the voters and cash Republicans were counting on.

Why it matters is that Kennedy's voters were a real part of the 2024 Trump coalition, especially in close states. If MAHA enthusiasm and money stay on the sidelines in the final ten days, Republican candidates lose both a funding stream and a slice of turnout they had assumed would be there.

items.title: Obama's second rally of the day lands in Detroit as Michigan opens early voting in a Senate race that could decide control
items.summary:
Hours after leaving Cleveland, former President Barack Obama was due on stage Saturday evening at Cass Technical High School in Detroit, rallying for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson. The gym was full well before the 5 p.m. start, with hundreds of supporters gathered outside, on the first day of Michigan's statewide in-person early voting period.

El-Sayed, a progressive who beat Representative Haley Stevens by less than a percentage point in the August primary, faces former Congressman Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat. The primary exposed real divisions — Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer backed Stevens, while Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez backed El-Sayed, and some primary ads even used Obama praising Stevens — so Saturday's joint appearance is as much a unity show as a turnout event.

Michigan is one of the few states that can plausibly decide both a governor's race and Senate control on November 3, which is why both parties are spending the final stretch there. President Donald Trump is scheduled to rally in St. Clair County on Sunday, giving Michigan back-to-back closing arguments from the two parties' biggest draws.

What to watch is Detroit itself. El-Sayed underperformed with Black voters in the city during the primary, and his campaign needs that base to turn out early and in force. Whether Obama's appeal transfers to a nominee who once sharply criticized Obama's record on war, deportations and Wall Street will be visible in the city's early-vote numbers this week.

items.title: Dow drops 652 points as oil tops $100 and investors brace for the Fed
items.summary:
Wall Street ended a volatile week lower on Friday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 652 points to 52,215 as U.S. oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel. The S&P 500 lost 39 points to 7,623 and the Nasdaq slipped 53 points to 25,955, a much smaller decline as technology shares steadied after earlier selling.

The move was driven by energy, not earnings alone. December Brent crude settled around $116.72 a barrel and U.S. crude around $103.27, both at five-month highs, as attacks and supply risks tied to the U.S.-Iran conflict tightened expectations for Middle East exports. The selling on Friday spread beyond growth stocks into defensive and financial names, and American Express fell more than 3% after its own restructuring news.

Expensive oil matters because it works like a tax on everything else. It raises fuel and shipping costs, feeds inflation, and makes it harder for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates even if growth slows. That is why a geopolitical oil shock quickly becomes a stock, bond and household-budget story.

What to watch next is a crowded week: the Fed decides on Wednesday, October 28, with markets broadly expecting no change, and Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon report earnings that will test whether huge AI spending is producing enough cloud and advertising revenue to justify it.

items.title: American Express cuts about 5% of staff to prepare for AI, even after record revenue
items.summary:
American Express said it will eliminate about 5% of its global workforce, roughly 3,500 people from a staff of nearly 77,000 at the end of 2025, and took a $336 million restructuring charge in the third quarter. Chief Executive Stephen Squeri disclosed the plan on the earnings call, and the finance chief described the goal as making the company leaner and more agile while preparing for AI.

The cuts did not follow a weak quarter. Amex reported record quarterly revenue of about $20.1 billion, up 9% from a year earlier, billed business of $454 billion, and adjusted earnings that beat analyst expectations. It also raised its full-year earnings outlook at the same time it announced the restructuring.

Managers said the sequence is deliberate: reduce management layers and widen spans of control first, then automate processes that have been simplified. Executives also stressed limits for outside AI assistants, saying agents would only be allowed into Amex systems through approved channels rather than being left to roam customer accounts.

The stakes go beyond one card company. Amex is offering a template other large employers are likely to copy — use a strong quarter to pay for job cuts framed as AI preparation, rather than waiting for a downturn. Investors punished the stock on Friday anyway, sending it down more than 3% and helping drag the Dow lower.

items.title: Big banks are now planning for the day after an AI catastrophe
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks are drafting contingency plans for a serious AI-related incident, according to Axios reporting summarized on October 24, moving beyond trying to prevent problems to planning how they would protect accounts, restore customer access and keep operating afterward. Institutions named in the coverage include Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America.

The immediate worry is more concrete than a runaway model. Customers are handing login credentials to third-party AI agents, and banks say it can be hard to tell whether an action inside an account was actually authorized by the customer or initiated by software acting on its own, at machine speed and around the clock. Several banks have already restricted or blocked outside agents from logging in and transacting directly.

Banks stress they have not found evidence of runaway agents or hacker attacks taking customer funds. The planning is precautionary, but the precaution itself is telling: the largest financial firms now treat agentic AI the way they treat cyberattacks or market shocks, as a scenario that needs a recovery playbook, not just a policy.

What to watch is whether banks, regulators and AI companies settle on a shared way to identify an agent, prove what a customer actually asked it to do, and reverse unauthorized actions quickly. Until that exists, expect more limits on agent access even as banks sell their own AI tools.

items.title: Treasury proposes wider ban on U.S. tech investment in China and other adversaries
items.summary:
The Treasury Department has proposed a rule to tighten restrictions on American investment in sensitive technology in China, Russia, North Korea and other countries of concern. The proposal covers areas such as artificial intelligence, supercomputing and other high-end capabilities that Washington does not want U.S. capital helping rivals build.

The effort builds on a program that began in 2023, when an executive order first restricted outbound investment in semiconductors, quantum computing and AI going into China, and Treasury created an outbound investment screening program. Congress then passed a law in December 2025 that codified the program and expanded it to more technologies and more countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The new proposal would push the boundaries further, adding areas such as hypersonic systems that travel at five times the speed of sound, biotechnology and expanded supercomputing and AI categories. It arrives just days after the administration waived some sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal, underscoring how economic tools are being adjusted country by country.

For investors and startups, the practical effect is more diligence and more deals that need government review or may be blocked outright. Supporters say capital can build military capability just as surely as exported hardware can; critics in business will be watching the comment period for how broadly the final rule is written.

items.title: Heating oil above $6 a gallon turns the Iran war into a winter bill at home
items.summary:
Heating oil has climbed above $6 a gallon nationally, up from about $3.50 a year ago, according to federal energy data cited by Reuters, and the increase is hitting hardest in northern states that still rely heavily on the fuel. In New Hampshire, one longtime Republican voter told Reuters he plans to lean on a wood stove this winter and vote for the Democratic Senate candidate because fuel costs have become so difficult.

Democrats are tying the prices directly to the war with Iran, which disrupted global diesel supplies; diesel, a close cousin of heating oil, hit a record above $6.50 a gallon. The Energy Department released heating oil from reserves in the Northeast this week, a move the White House pointed to in response, though an analyst said the release was unlikely to move prices much on its own.

The politics are sharpest where the Senate is closest. Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska all have competitive November 3 races that could help decide control of Congress, and all are exposed to heating and fuel costs. A Republican strategist in Maine acknowledged the basic problem: voters tend to hold the party in power responsible, especially when the cause is easy to connect to a president's war.

What to watch is whether reserve releases, any shift in the Iran conflict, or a break in diesel prices arrives before cold weather and Election Day converge. If prices stay near $6, energy will remain both a household squeeze and one of the clearest ways foreign policy is showing up in American voters' pocketbooks.

items.title: Mississippi officer who shot a 1-year-old and the interim chief both resign
items.summary:
The Senatobia, Mississippi police officer who fatally shot 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot in June has resigned, and the city's interim police chief has also stepped down, local officials said on Friday. Mayor Greg Graves confirmed officer Hunter Foster's resignation without saying whether he was asked to leave.

The shooting happened on June 14 during a response to a shoplifting call. Investigators said officers encountered two adults and a child fleeing into a vehicle, tried to stop it, and an officer fired as the vehicle drove in their direction and then fled. Body-camera video released this week shows officers shouting for the car to stop and Foster firing into the passenger side, where the child was on his mother's lap.

Foster's resignation came days after Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch cleared him of criminal wrongdoing and said the use of force was justified. His lawyer said he resigned for the good of the city and the department and to allow healing. The child's family disputes that the shooting was justified.

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, representing the family, said accountability cannot end with a resignation and called for a Justice Department investigation. The department has already been through other turmoil, including the firing of its former chief last month, so what to watch is who leads Senatobia police next and whether federal reviewers take up the case.

items.title: Citizenship applicants swept up in California illegal-voting crackdown
items.summary:
Most of the immigrants charged in California this week for alleged illegal voting or registration had applied for U.S. citizenship, and now face charges tied to lying on forms or in interviews that could bring prison time and end their naturalization cases. Federal authorities charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents on Monday, and by Thursday had filed detailed charging documents in 10 of 28 cases.

One man, Jose Antonio Banuelos-Diaz, 42, has lived in the United States for 40 years and applied for citizenship in October 2025. Prosecutors allege he improperly claimed to be a citizen when registering to vote in 2007 and later lied about it on immigration paperwork, but they have not accused him of casting a ballot. He told the AP he did not know he was registered, recalled only getting a driver's license around that time — when California prompts license applicants about voter registration — and said he has never voted because he knows he cannot.

He was released after his arrest outside his Los Angeles home and faces up to five years in prison if convicted. His case illustrates how the crackdown is using old voter-registration data to build broader immigration-status charges, rather than focusing only on ballots actually cast.

The stakes are high for long-term residents whose citizenship applications brought them to the government's attention in the first place. What to watch is how many of the 28 cases produce convictions or deportations, and whether courts accept mistakes at the motor-vehicle counter, nearly 20 years later, as proof of intentional false claims.

items.title: Hurricane Vance slows off Mexico's Pacific coast after briefly reaching major strength
items.summary:
Hurricane Vance rapidly strengthened off Mexico's Pacific coast, reaching maximum sustained winds of about 110 mph as it churned several hundred miles south-southwest of Acapulco, according to the National Hurricane Center. Forecasters expected gradual weakening to begin by Saturday as the storm encountered cooler water and drier air.

Vance was moving slowly northwest, a track expected to continue through the weekend and bring it closer to the Puerto Vallarta area by Monday if it holds enough strength. Its outer bands were already pushing gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico's Gulf of Tehuantepec, and forecasters warned of life-threatening surf and rip currents along the southern and southwestern coast.

The storm caps an intense Pacific season shaped by strong El Nino conditions, with hurricanes forming in quick succession near Hawaii and Mexico. Vance became the seventh major hurricane in a row in the basin this year, after Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy, and the first V-named eastern Pacific storm since 2018.

What to watch is the slow movement, which makes the forecast less certain than usual. A stronger Vance would track closer to shore; a weaker one could turn farther west and stay offshore. Either way, coastal communities should expect dangerous seas through the weekend and into next week.

items.title: Nashville SC beats Montreal 2-0 to win its first Supporters' Shield
items.summary:
Nashville SC clinched the MLS Supporters' Shield on Saturday with a 2-0 win at CF Montreal, securing the best regular-season record in the league for the first time in club history. Sam Surridge and Hany Mukhtar scored in the second half, and goalkeeper Brian Schwake made five saves.

After a scoreless first half, Surridge opened the scoring in the 52nd minute by putting away his own rebound after his header was parried by 17-year-old Montreal goalkeeper Samsy Keita, who was making his MLS debut. Mukhtar doubled the lead in the 76th minute, intercepting a misplayed pass in Montreal's defensive third and finishing from close range.

Nashville improved to 21-3-7 with 70 points, extending its unbeaten run to seven matches and sitting just four points shy of the league record set by Miami in 2025, with matches still to play. Schwake's shutout was his league-leading 14th of the season, while Montreal, at 6-18-7, was eliminated from playoff contention.

The Shield is Nashville's second major trophy, following last season's U.S. Open Cup, and it brings home-field advantage throughout the MLS Cup playoffs plus a berth in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup. What to watch is whether Nashville can chase down the points record in its final three regular-season matches without risking its top players before the playoffs.

items.title: After the Bend school shooting, the question is whether a parent will be charged
items.summary:
Nine days after a gunman opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three students and a teacher, attention is turning to whether a parent of the teenage suspect could face criminal charges. The October 15 attack killed Rhoam Summer, 5, two boys ages 8 and 11, and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, and wounded another teacher and a 7-year-old girl before the 16-year-old suspect was tackled by a teacher and killed by an armed bystander.

Police have said the Maverick 88 pump-action shotgun used in the shooting was legally purchased, but have not said by whom; several outlets have reported, citing unnamed law enforcement sources, that the suspect's mother bought it. Bend police declined to confirm that, and detectives have served search warrants on the suspect's home, devices and social media accounts. A legal team hired by Rhoam Summer's family is running its own investigation, including into how the weapon was stored.

Oregon has no law written specifically to punish parents when a child uses their gun, though legal experts say charges such as manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide or child neglect are possible depending on the facts. Its safe-storage law carries only a fine, and professors who have studied parent prosecutions say a homicide case would be hard without evidence of ignored warning signs — the kind of red flags that underpinned the convictions of the Crumbleys in Michigan and Colin Gray in Georgia.

Watch for what the Bend investigation finds about warning signs and the gun's storage, and whether prosecutors test Oregon law with charges that would stretch the Michigan and Georgia precedents.

items.title: Obama rallies thousands in Cleveland for Brown and Acton, blasting Trump and the Ramaswamy mother ad
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama campaigned in Cleveland on Saturday, October 24, joining former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton at Cleveland Public Auditorium. It was Obama's first trip to Ohio since 2018, and it came with both Brown and Acton locked in tight races ahead of the November 3 election.

Speaking to thousands of supporters, Obama argued that voters are not stuck with what he called a spineless Congress and Republican governors enabling the Trump administration, and he blamed the president for rising costs while criticizing immigration and foreign policy moves. He portrayed Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy as an opportunist and Sen. Jon Husted as a rubber stamp, and he also condemned a Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, saying no office is worth stooping that low. Ramaswamy has kept the ad up despite a call from Gov. Mike DeWine to remove it, and his campaign answered Obama by attacking Acton and the Affordable Care Act.

The stakes are unusually high for a midterm in Ohio. Brown's race against Husted, who holds the seat once held by Vice President JD Vance, could help determine control of the U.S. Senate, and Acton is trying to put a Democrat in the governor's office for the first time since 2011. Acton told the crowd her opponent is out for himself, while Brown said national media will never write off Ohio again.

What to watch is whether the rally moves turnout in Cuyahoga County during the final week of early voting. Obama was also headed to Detroit the same day, underscoring how much national Democrats are investing in the Great Lakes in the closing stretch.

items.title: Ohio early voting tops 920,000 ballots returned as first Saturday voting opens
items.summary:
Ohio's early vote kept climbing into the weekend, with state data as of October 23 showing 922,793 ballots already returned. That total comes from 1,240,470 early ballots issued, including 527,760 people who have voted in person and 395,033 mail ballots returned out of 712,710 sent.

Saturday, October 24, marked the start of weekend early voting, with boards of elections open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Hours expand sharply in the final week, running longer on weekdays before early in-person voting ends on November 1. The November 3 election is headlined by the Acton-Ramaswamy governor's race and the Brown-Husted Senate race.

The returned ballots already represent about 11.2 percent of the roughly 8.2 million registered voters Ohio counted in 2024. County officials in places such as Franklin and Licking counties have said the pace is well ahead of the 2022 and 2018 midterms, driven by competitive statewide races and growing preference for voting in person over mail.

What to watch is the final-week surge. Both parties are watching whether the high early pace holds through October 31 and November 1, and whether mail ballots returned by the 7:30 p.m. Election Day deadline narrow or widen the early picture.

items.title: University Hospitals MyChart still offline into the weekend after unusual server activity
items.summary:
Cleveland-based University Hospitals remained in a precautionary digital shutdown heading into the weekend, after detecting unusual activity on its servers on October 22 and disconnecting systems from the internet. The outage has taken the MyChart patient portal and parts of the public website offline.

UH has said there is currently no impact on patient care delivery, and that staff are working around the clock with outside experts to determine the scope of the problem. The system has warned that digital disruptions could continue for the next few days, and it has directed patients to call their provider's office for test results and appointments, or call 866-844-2273 to schedule.

No restoration announcement had been reported by Saturday evening, and UH has not said whether the activity was a cyberattack or whether any patient data was exposed. The 18-hospital system completed a move to Epic in 2023 that consolidated about 5.6 million patient records and scheduling systems.

For patients, the practical effect is phone-first access until MyChart returns. What to watch is a UH update on which systems are restored, how long the investigation lasts, and whether the system eventually characterizes what triggered the shutdown.

items.title: Cleveland VA goes live on the new federal electronic health record on October 24
items.source: Wisevoter / VA Northeast Ohio Healthcare System
items.summary:
The Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center and its Northeast Ohio clinics were scheduled to go live on Saturday, October 24, on the Federal Electronic Health Record, the Oracle-based system the Department of Veterans Affairs shares with the Department of Defense. VA leaders marked the moment with a "Cleveland Rocks" kickoff on October 23.

The new system is meant to replace the VA's decades-old VistA records, which varied from facility to facility and did not easily talk to Defense Department hospitals. Supporters say a single record should follow a veteran from military service into VA care, with tools to help staff organize charts, notes, and care plans. Cleveland is going live alongside Anchorage as the final 2026 deployments, after earlier Ohio, Michigan, and Indiana sites.

The rollout carries a difficult history. The national program began in 2018, was paused in April 2023 over safety and workflow concerns, and has grown well beyond its original $10 billion contract, drawing congressional scrutiny and a recent vote to subpoena Oracle executives over costs. Protesters at the Cleveland facility raised concerns about integration and the loss of institutional knowledge during the switch.

Veterans in Northeast Ohio should check that histories, referrals, and care plans carried over correctly during the changeover, when extra in-person technical support is on site. What to watch is whether Cleveland avoids the referral backlogs and slowdowns reported at some earlier sites.

items.title: Cleveland extends its data center moratorium through January as Ohio towns put data centers on the ballot
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council has extended the city's moratorium on data center permits, giving officials until January 29, 2027, or until new permanent rules take effect, to write regulations for an industry that can place heavy demands on electricity, water, and land. The pause covers review and issuance of use, building, and zoning permits and other licenses for data centers across the city.

Council members said existing data centers are not currently subject to specific city rules on zoning, utility use, or noise, and a Data Center Working Group of industry experts, utility representatives, residents, and city officials is studying approaches used in Ohio and elsewhere. Councilman Brian Kazy said the goal is not to drive away businesses that have caused no problems, while other members opposed large mega centers without guardrails.

Cleveland is part of a much wider Ohio fight. Voters in at least 18 Ohio communities will decide data center measures on November 3, including proposed charter amendments in Pataskala, Sunbury, and Granville that would ban facilities over 25 megawatts, and a statewide signature effort aiming for a similar constitutional ban in 2027.

Why it matters locally is the power bill and the grid. Residents at Cleveland town halls raised concerns about reliability and water use, and state polling cited in the debate shows most Ohio voters do not want a large data center in their own community. What to watch is the permanent Cleveland ordinance the working group produces before the January deadline.

items.title: Case Western law clinic wins court ruling that preserves Ohio clean air protections
items.summary:
A Franklin County court has struck down provisions in Ohio's 2025 budget bill that would have weakened clean air protections and restricted the use of air quality data collected by communities themselves. Case Western Reserve University School of Law's Environmental Law Clinic helped bring the case, with director Miranda Leppla representing the Ohio Environmental Council and the Sierra Club.

The court ruled the provisions violated Ohio's constitutional one-subject rule because they were not rationally related to appropriations or agency operations. It severed them from the law, barred Ohio EPA from further action to remove the Air Nuisance Rule from the state's clean air plan, and ordered the agency to withdraw its pending request to federal EPA to remove the rule.

The Air Nuisance Rule has for decades let Ohioans challenge pollution near industrial facilities, and the struck provisions would also have barred data from community-operated air monitors, which residents use where government monitoring is limited. The plaintiffs included residents living near steel plants in Middletown and Youngstown and Licking County residents who built their own monitoring networks.

The ruling means Ohioans keep both the nuisance tool and the ability to use community monitoring data to document pollution and seek enforcement. Leppla said major policy changes should get public debate on their own merits rather than being tucked into a must-pass budget, a principle the court has now enforced in this case.

baby.tip: Car seat week: install the base in the Acura now, while there's no rush, and practice clicking the Aria in and out and adjusting the harness a few times. If you want a second set of eyes, many local fire departments and hospitals offer free car seat checks — worth booking before the baby arrives, and anything you are unsure about is a good question for your OB's office or the pediatrician's office.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding only a teaspoon or so at a time, and it grows to about the size of an egg by the end of the first month. That's why newborns feed so often in small amounts at first: frequent feeding is the design, not a problem.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: build the 'first ride home' playlist together — one song pick each from Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents. Save it on both phones so it's ready for the drive home from the hospital, whatever day that turns out to be.
